query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a nanoscale, in‐situ forming lubricious phase into the CoCrFeNi matrix—by, for example, dispersing a small volume fraction of WS2 particles—will generate a stable, low‐shear tribolayer during sliding that maintains low friction and reduced wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix that in its as-processed state lacks inherent self‐lubricating phases.
generation.intervention: Dispersion of nanoscale WS2 (or a similar solid lubricant) into the alloy, such that during sliding contact the lubricant phase forms a protective, low-shear tribofilm.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under variable load and environmental conditions, with temperatures continuously varied from ambient up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform distribution of WS2 particles facilitates in-situ formation of a lubricious tribolayer at the contact interface, which persists over the operating temperature range.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the dispersed WS2 particles interact with the CoCrFeNi matrix and, under mechanical and thermal activation, form a thin lubricious film. This film reduces interfacial shear by providing easy-shear basal planes (and possibly adapts its crystal structure slightly at higher temperatures) that counteract the tendency for friction and wear to increase, even as the matrix experiences temperature-induced microstructural changes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, the WS2-enhanced alloy is predicted to maintain a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate consistently across the tested temperature range. There may be minor differences at room temperature, but the gap should widen under elevated temperatures near 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNi alloy without lubricant addition, which shows increasing friction and wear due to its temperature-dependent microstructural evolution.
generation.boundary: The proposed benefit is expected provided that the added WS2 remains chemically stable and does not oxidize into a non-lubricious phase under the applied loads and environmental oxygen levels. Extreme oxidative conditions or excessive loads that could disrupt the integrity of the lubricious film would lie outside the effective range of this intervention.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal volume fraction, dispersion uniformity, and high-temperature chemical stability of WS2 in the CoCrFeNi matrix are not yet firmly established and require experimental validation. It is also uncertain whether similar lubricious behavior would persist under all practical loading and environmental variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one with the standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy and one with an identical alloy composition but with a controlled addition (e.g., 5 vol%) of nanoscale WS2. Perform standardized sliding wear tests from room temperature to 800 °C under identical applied loads and environmental conditions. Use in-situ monitoring and post-test microstructural analyses.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate (via mass loss or wear track dimensions)
Tribolayer morphology and composition (using SEM/TEM and XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WS2-modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the coefficient of friction and wear rate over the temperature range compared to the baseline alloy, or if the lubricious tribofilm is not observed or degrades under test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. At 300 K and 600 K, the ordered lattice structure of the high entropy alloy coating material is basically the same, and thus its hardness is basically the same. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.
